title: The slave trade and the Church
hookLine: popes condemned it, and yet Catholics took part; Gregory XVI condemned the trade outright in 1839

lines: A PRIEST GOES DOWN INTO THE HOLD.
cards: A ship docks at Cartagena, on the Caribbean coast of South America. In its hold are African men, women and children, chained, sick and terrified.

On the dock a Spanish Jesuit waits with water, fruit, bandages and interpreters, and he goes down into the hold. His name is Peter Claver, and he called himself, in Latin, the servant of the Africans forever.
He cared for the people the ships brought for the rest of his life. And the ships kept coming, into a Catholic city, bought and sold by baptized men.

teach.b: This is a hard story, told in four parts. First, the permission. Earlier popes had issued letters granting Portugal's kings the right to conquer non-Christian lands and to reduce their peoples to servitude.
Some historians read those letters as part of how the Atlantic trade grew. Second, the protests.
Other popes and Catholics spoke against enslaving Indigenous peoples and Africans: priests like Claver, a few theologians, and popes in letters of their own. Third, the practice.
Catholic merchants, colonists, and even religious orders and dioceses held enslaved people, bought them and sold them.
In the United States, Jesuits in Maryland sold the people they held to pay their debts, and their descendants are still telling that story today. Fourth, the letter.

Pope Gregory the Sixteenth, in a letter of eighteen thirty-nine, recalled the earlier condemnations and forbade any cleric or layperson to defend the trade in Africans as permissible, or to preach or teach it in any way.
Even then, some Catholics read his words as condemning the trade but not slavery itself, and went on as before. Condemned and still done.
Saint Paul writes to the Galatians, in the Douay-Rheims: "There is neither Jew nor Greek: there is neither bond nor free." The words were there all along.
Some Catholics today name this history as a wound, and a warning that a church can say the right thing and still fail to live it.

how: Catholics remember Peter Claver on his feast day, and some American dioceses and religious orders, including Jesuits, have studied and publicly acknowledged their own past in slavery, working with descendants on reconciliation.

practice: Bring to mind the people carried on those ships, whose names most people will never know. You don't have to picture the details; just let them be people, with mothers and children and songs.
If you pray, pray for them and for their descendants today; if you don't, hold them in silence.
